clinician.trajectory_summary: A 79-year-old woman with hypertension and mild Alzheimer’s dementia presented with acute loss of consciousness and presumed cardiac arrest, requiring CPR and intubation. Initial GCS was 3. Early workup including CT brain, CT angiogram, routine blood tests, telemetry, and EEG were unremarkable. Despite initial negative brain imaging, the patient remained neurologically impaired. An echocardiogram later showed concentric left ventricular wall thickening suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis, and hematological work-up revealed raised lambda light chains and Bence-Jones proteinuria, indicative of a plasma cell disorder. An MRI of the brain, performed 72 hours after symptom onset, revealed symmetrical, bilateral thalamic diffusion restriction consistent with an AOP infarction. The patient's GCS improved to 13-14, but she had persistent cognitive impairment, disorientation, and a vertical gaze palsy. She was discharged to a stroke rehabilitation center 11 days after her stroke.
